 Order

The first accused in C.C.No.180 of 1996 on the files of the Court of the Judicial Magistrate of First Class, Payyannur, filed this revision petition challenging the concurrent finding of conviction and sentence passed by the courts below under Sections 16 (1A) (i) r/w Section 2(ia) (h) and 7 (i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act r/w Rule 47 Appendix B.A 07.04.01 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules and Section 16 (1) (a) (ii) and 7(iii) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act and Rule 50 (1) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules and Rule 10 of the Kerala PFA Rules.

entities.text: Judicial Magistrate of First Class, Payyannur
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text:
2. Heard.
3.
The prosecution allegation can be briefly stated thus:-
On 29.11.1995 at about 2.45 p.m., PW1, the Food Inspector purchased 900 gram of ice candy from the first accused.
The second accused was the owner of the said shop.
After sampling as per rules, one sample was sent to the Public Analyst for analysis.
After analysis, the Public Analyst submitted Ext.P12 report stating that the sample contained artificial sweeteners saccharine and dulcin and was therefore adulterated.
Thereafter, on the request of the accused, the second sample was sent to the Central Food Laboratory for analysis.
Ext.P17 certificate of the Central Food Laboratory would show that the sample did not conform to the standard prescribed for ice candy as per the PFA Rules and was therefore adulterated.
4. Before the trial Court, PW1 to PW4 were examined and Exts.P1 to P23 were marked for the prosecution.
DW1 was examined and Exts.D1 to D6 were marked for the revision petitioner.

5. The learned counsel for the revision petitioner has submitted that since no laboratory for the analysis of the food item was defined and no validated method of analysis was prescribed as per the mandate of Section 23 (1-A)(ee) and (hh) of the PFA Act, Ext.P17 cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased by the Food Inspector was adulterated.
The learned counsel for the revision petitioner relied on the decision of the Apex Court in Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176] to buttress his argument.

entities.text: Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
A.P.Abdul Salam vs State - Represented By The Public on 8 February, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/191628373/
2 6.

In this case, admittedly, the laboratory for the analysis of food item was not defined and no validated method of analysis of the food item was specified as mandated under Section 23 (1-A) (ee)
and (hh) of the P.F.A. Act.

Therefore, Ext. P17 certificate of analysis cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased in this case was adulterated in view of the decision of the Apex court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra).

It was held by the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra)
that since the Laboratories were not notified and the tests conducted by such laboratories were not admissible in evidence, no prosecution could be based on such report and the accused was entitled to get acquittal.

In the decision of this Court in Gopalakrishnan v. Food Inspector [2013 (3) KLT 455], the court relied on the decision of the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) and found that the Public Analyst's report was not admissible in evidence and accordingly, the Court acquitted the accused.
The matter was referred to a Division Bench and the Division Bench also affirmed the said decision, submitted by the learned counsel for the petitioner and the learned Public Prosecutor.

Even otherwise, in view of the decision in Pepsico India Holdings (supra), the conviction in this case cannot be sustained as no laboratory was notified and no validated method of analysis was specified as mandated under Section 23 (1-A) (ee) and (hh) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.

In the said circumstances, the concurrent finding of conviction and sentence passed by the courts below under Section 16 (1A) (i) r/w Sections 2(ia) (h) and 7 (i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act r/w Rule 47 Appendix B.A 07.04.01 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules cannot be sustained and consequently, I set aside the same.
7. Both the courts concurrently found that the revision petitioner did not have the requisite licence under the PFA Rules to sell the food item.

Having gone through the relevant inputs, I do not find any reason to hold that the appreciation of evidence or the concurrent finding by the courts below in this regard suffers from any infirmity warranting interference by this Court.

In the said circumstances, the concurrent finding by the courts below that the revision petitioner sold the food item without having a valid licence under the PFA Rules does not warrant any interference by this Court.
8. As regards the sentence, the learned counsel for the revision petitioner has pleaded for leniency.
The revision petitioner was aged only 18 years during the relevant period.
The revision petitioner is presently aged 39 years.

Considering the facts and circumstances of the case, including the age of the revision petitioner during the relevant period, I am of the view that this is a fit case where the sentence can be awarded as provided under the second proviso to Section 16 (1) of the PFA Act and accordingly, the revision petitioner is sentenced to imprisonment till the rising of the court and a fine of Rs.500/- (Rupees five hundred only) and in default to simple imprisonment for ten days under Sections 16 (1) (a) (ii) and 7 (iii) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act r/w Rule 50 (1) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules and Rule 10 of the Kerala PFA Rules, to secure the ends of Justice.
In the result, this revision petition stands allowed in part as above.
The revision petitioner shall surrender before the trial court on 1.4.2016 to suffer the sentence.
